My name is Vanjie Garcia, Transportation Planning and Programming Manager in Public Works. The effort of updating the ADA transition plan for public rights-of-way began last year. The City adopted a previous plan in 2015, and we now have an official draft update to that plan, concluding with a public hearing tonight. Tonight's presentation will provide you some document highlights. This is intended to be a review of the journey developing this plan. A copy of the full document was included in the agenda. The plan is also available at RentonADA.com, where the online document has been formatted to be used with assisted reading technologies. When the ADA was signed into law, a transition plan is required of public entities to ensure their facilities meet accessibility standards. The U.S. Access Board is responsible for developing and updating standards for accessible design, otherwise known as the ADAG manual, or ADAG for short. These guidelines are used by the Department of Justice and the Department of Transportation in setting enforceable standards. This transition plan addresses barriers to pedestrian facilities within public rights-of-way, which are usually under the purview of the public works or transportation departments at most agencies. These are examples of the types of barriers that are typically addressed in a transition plan for public rights-of-way. The City inventoried existing physical barriers in GIS, conducted a public survey online, and provided a mail-in option. The public feedback included focus groups of both external and internal stakeholders. The previous plan from 2015 created a thoughtful baseline in addressing access needs, but there were some important parts that needed more detail, such as a schedule and timeline for implementation and stakeholder input. In the last few decades, many public agencies have increased efforts in creating or updating transition plans, partly because of legal action that has occurred in other jurisdictions. In some circumstances, a sponsor agency is required to have a transition plan in order to apply for a grant or is at a severe disadvantage. This update includes recommendations after conducting a policy and process audit from our consultant, who has developed transition plans for multiple jurisdictions. I will go over the prioritization results from the self-evaluation in the next few slides. The stakeholder engagement strategy included an online open house with mail-in forms provided to community partners. Due to the pandemic, the outreach sessions had to be online instead of in-person and included meetings with the Senior Advisory Committee and Lighthouse for the Blind. One of the most important deliverables from this update is a GIS map portal to help track progress of burial removal after this plan is adopted. When Renton became an AARP age-friendly city, we committed to creating a plan to address the eight domains of livability. The ADA transition plan process directly aligns with the transportation domain under this initiative in helping create a place that helps people of all ages get to where they need to go, regardless of travel mode and ability. The city increases the livability index of Renton. 17% of existing ramps are ADA compliant and 9% have minor compliance issues, which leaves the rest of the 4,000 plus curb ramps having significant compliance issues. Curb ramps are designed and constructed to tie into existing roadways. Steep or otherwise constrained locations may make it infeasible to meet ADA grade standards. When not feasible to remove all curb ramp barriers, ramps may be built to the maximum extent feasible to satisfy ADA requirements, but specific documentation called MEFs are required. These numbers do not account for ramps with MEFs. Approximately 353 miles of sidewalk were inventoried with approximately 49% in compliance with ADA standards. The self-evaluation process allowed the city to inventory existing barriers and it was only a starting point. This plan also looked at other parameters such as sidewalk widths and whether signalized intersection had audible push buttons. Assessing all these access needs can be overwhelming and having a current ADA transition plan is a way for a city to plan forward. Since the data for this plan was collected between 2019 to early 2020, some of the barriers identified in this document have been addressed through new construction. Downtown is a great example. The ADA requires the transition plan to specify a schedule for taking steps to make existing facilities ADA compliant. This includes creating a prioritization process and framework. Our plan consisted of a GIS process that scored all the barriers due to one, physical impact to accessibility and two, proximity to key pedestrian destinations. Those scores resulted in these maps. The higher the score, the higher the priority for the city to address. The existing transportation program funding levels, this analysis resulted in approximately 135 years to remove all the very high priority barriers within city right-of-way. However, this analysis only evaluated existing transportation programs and does not include discrete capital projects that will be constructed by other departments or even transportation or private development when it comes in. Chapter five of this plan document includes recommended actions that are required for agencies to do in a transition plan as noted in the ADA, as well as others that have resulted from the policy audit, the external outreach, and the internal listening sessions. Chapter five goes into more detail into each recommendation and suggested next steps. Recommendation number 11 comes into trying to reduce the 135 years calculated to address all the high priority barriers. It recommends an additional two hundred and forty thousand dollars per year for the next 50 years in order to remove the high priority barriers identified in the self-evaluation. The ADA transition plan is meant to be a living document. This is a progression from the previous 2015 version. Once adopted, we have recommendations and action steps to move closer to becoming a barrier-free city for all. Today is the close of the public comment period that began at the end of October.
